newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says Bundesbank move important ahead of EMU.
newsitem.headline: Waigel says Bundesbank move important ahead of EMU.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Thursday welcomed the Bundesbank's decision to free repurchase transactions from minimum reserve requirements, saying the move would boost Germany as a financial centre.
In a statement, Waigel said, "Additionally...the Bundesbank is tailoring its reserve instrument to the competitive conditions in international money and capital markets.

"The abolition of the reserve requirement is an important step in the run-up to European monetary union which adjusts the reserve instrument to the future demands of a stability-oriented monetary policy," he said.
Earlier, the Bundesbank said it would exempt repurchase agreements with maturities of up to one year from minimum reserve requirements from January 1, 1997.

Commercial banks had long lobbied the Bundesbank to abolish its requirement that reserves must be held on repurchase agreements conducted between credit institutions or banks and non-banks, saying this hurt German banks' competitiveness.

Despite the small cutback in its reserve requirements, the central bank said it still viewed minimum reserves as an important monetary instrument and would continue to push for their use by the future European Central Bank.

In his statement, Waigel noted that the decision continued a process of adjustment in minimum reserves but did not weaken reserves as a policy tool. "The core functions of the minimum reserve are being retained," he said.
